messages.author: a321e6ab7b0cca0d
messages.subject: Add markers to a map
parts:
Dear list,

I would like to add various markers to this map:

library(maptools)
library(ggplot2)
gpclibPermit()

myshp <- readShapeSpatial(system.file("shapes/sids.shp",
package="maptools"))
myshp.p<- fortify.SpatialPolygonsDataFrame(myshp, region="CNTY_ID")
shpm<- merge(myshp.p, myshp, by.x="id", by.y="CNTY_ID")
p <- ggplot(shpm, aes(long,lat,group=group))
p <- p + geom_polygon(fill="dodgerblue1") + geom_path(color="white")
p <- p + coord_equal()
p

In this map I want to place e.g. this cities

#long lat
-78.644722, 35.818889 - Raleigh
-80.843333, 35.226944 - Charlotte
-82.555833, 35.58 - Asheville

Any ideas?
Thanks for any help!
Patrick

messages.author: 4e69b94a09c8cf3b
messages.subject: Re: Add markers to a map
parts:
I generally add a geom_point pointing to a data frame containing the
additional locations. Something along the lines of

geom_points(aes(group=NULL),data=cities,shape=3,color="white").

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Add markers to a map
parts:
Hi:

Based on Mark's useful answer, I was curious how to plot city labels in place of the points, and came up with this.

cities <- read.table(textConnection("
long        lat      city
-78.644722 35.818889  Raleigh
-80.843333 35.226944  Charlotte
-82.555833 35.58      Asheville"), header = TRUE)

p + geom_text(aes(group = NULL, lab = city), data = cities, size = 3, color = 'white')

If you want both, which wouldn't be unreasonable, you'd need to offset the city labels a bit by adjusting the lat/long values.

BTW, Mark made a little typo - he meant geom_point(). And I'm wondering why you chose Dodger Blue (LA!) instead of Carolina blue :)  A little trip to Google, and...
http://www.december.com/html/spec/color3.html

p <- ggplot(shpm, aes(long,lat,group=group))
p <- p + geom_polygon(fill="#539DC2") + geom_path(color="white")

p <- p + coord_equal()
p

Voila! Carolina blue. I couldn't resist :) 

HTH,
Dennis

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Add markers to a map
parts:
Hi Mark:

I'm not a geo guy like you are, so I appreciate the tips. I like your color choice. (See the attachment.) My little joke was that since the state is North Carolina and the color that Patrick used was Dodger blue, why not put in Carolina blue instead? (The colors of the athletic teams from the University of North Carolina (the 'Tar Heels') are (supposed to be!) Carolina blue and white, so I actually did intend for the map to be in those colors, with apologies to Duke and NC State grads on the list :)    http://tarheelblue.cstv.com/
(I actually think their colors are closer to skyblue1 or 2 than real Carolina blue; the web site above mentions 'Tar Heel blue', so I'll have to look that up, but I digress :)

What I like about your color choice is that if you insert text labels for the cities in white, they stand out much better, as do the borders. In my (and Patrick's) color scheme, I thought it would be necessary to darken the background to better see the Hatteras islands on the east coast of the state; your choices handle that problem well.  I've been saving some of your contributions to the list and Wiki with regard to spatial maps, so thanks for another useful lesson in applied cartography with ggplot2!

Cheers,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Add markers to a map
parts:
Two resources to look into (not just for county lines):
http://www2.census.gov/cgi-bin/shapefiles/national-files
http://seamless.usgs.gov/website/seamless/viewer.htm

Also, you are getting into the realm of projected and geographic coordinate systems.  Your plot of NC is by lat and long, but the way you are mapping without projecting is going to distort things pretty well.  If the units really are lat-long, you might want to re-project the shapefile into NC state plane coordinates (which will require that you know what the geographic coordinate system is) and compare the outputs of the two plots. 

Most of the downloads from the referenced sites will be projected as state plane coordinate systems appropriate to their locale, which will minimize distortion (of course states like Florida have to be uncooperative and have three state plane zones in the state).  The projected coordinate system will help make Paul's scale bar make sense in light of Hadley's admonition.  His scale bar on your map won't make too much good sense.  NC cooperates by being long rather than tall, which will naturally lessen the distortion from claiming the lat-long is a flat surface.  You can get away with even more when the map scale is large (mapping a small area).
